Jamaat could have resolved questions over its 1971 role with Razzaq’s 2016 statement: Asaduzzaman
2026-09-18T13:43:14+06:00 | Star Online Report
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/politics/news/jamaat-could-have-resolved-questions-over-its-1971-role-razzaqs-2016-statement-asaduzzaman-4276191

Many questions surrounding Jamaat-e-Islami's role in the 1971 Liberation War could have been resolved had the party accepted a draft statement prepared by its former assistant secretary general Abdur Razzaq in 2016, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman said today.

He described Razzaq’s position – that Jamaat should issue a statement to the nation addressing its role in 1971 – as “far-sighted.”

Asaduzzaman was speaking at the launch of Razzaq’s posthumously published book, “Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami: Its History and Politics”, published by University Press Limited (UPL), at Lakeshore Grand in Dhaka’s Gulshan.

DU must not be turned into a battleground for history

Razzaq’s two sons also spoke at the event, which was attended by his wife.

Referring to the National Freedom Fighters Council Act, the law minister said that when it was amended in 2026, the definition of freedom fighters included those who fought for Bangladesh's independence against the Pakistani occupation forces and their collaborators, including Razakars and Al-Badr, as well as the "then Jamaat-e-Islami", the "then Muslim League" and the "then Nizam-e-Islami".

He said Jamaat had sought the removal of its name when the amendment was discussed by a special parliamentary committee.

“From Jamaat’s side, they asked, ‘Can Jamaat’s name be removed from here?’” Asaduzzaman said.

“We replied, ‘We cannot deny the historical truth.’”

Following discussions, he said, the word “then” was added before the names of Jamaat-e-Islami, the Muslim League and Nizam-e-Islami.

Asaduzzaman said Jamaat did not vote against the amendment when it was placed before parliament.

“When this law was placed in parliament, you know that when a law is passed in parliament, there are ‘yes’ and ‘no’ votes. Jamaat-e-Islami did not cast any ‘no’ vote on this definition or this amendment. This is on record,” he said.

Asaduzzaman then linked the parliamentary process to Razzaq's efforts in 2016 to persuade Jamaat to address its 1971 role.

“Indirectly, Jamaat, by not voting ‘no’, accepted its role in 1971 through the parliamentary process. This was the same issue Barrister Razzaq tried to bring before the nation through a draft statement in 2016, based on his political thinking and principles,” he said.

“If Razzaq’s statement had been signed in 2016, many questions about Jamaat would have been resolved," the law minister said.

Razzaq's posthumous memoir details repeated efforts within Jamaat over the years to persuade the party leadership to address its role in opposing Bangladesh's independence. In November 2016, Razzaq prepared a draft statement that included an apology over the party's role in 1971.

Speaking about his relationship with Razzaq, Asaduzzaman said the two had strong ideological differences but maintained a close personal relationship. "...I was never in the same line with Razzaq, and I am still not," he said.

Asaduzzaman said Razzaq's advice had helped guide him, particularly during periods of political repression. "Especially during the time of fascism, Razzaq’s guidance was like a light showing me the way," he said.

The minister recalled that when the BNP appointed him as its human rights secretary, Razzaq had described the decision as "one of the most progressive steps" taken.

The law minister said Razzaq's book reflected his efforts to reform Jamaat and transform it from what he called the “circle of reactionary politics” into a “progressive Islamic political party”.

Asaduzzaman said that Razzaq believed Islamic rule should not be imposed from the top. Rather, a state could be shaped by Islamic values if those values developed within society.

The minister said he might disagree with Razzaq's idea of an Islamic state, but considered his approach appropriate from the perspective of a jurist.

Describing the book, Asaduzzaman said he did not see it simply as a work of literature or research. "This book seemed to me like a living encyclopedia of a person," he said.

The law minister also criticised senior Jamaat leaders and prominent Supreme Court lawyers associated with the party for not attending the event.

"I expected them to be here in today’s discussion. If they could not attend, it shows their weakness. It is their failure. It shows their narrowness and limitations." They could have attended and disagreed with Razzaq's views, he said.

"Because this is democracy," he said. He pointed out that Razzaq's book also contained criticism of the BNP.

"This book also criticises the BNP. Which is fine. We have to accept it," he said. The minister said society could not move forward without a political culture that allowed criticism and differing views.

Asaduzzaman said that although Razzaq served as an assistant secretary general of Jamaat, his work, ideas and standing went far beyond his position in the party. The law minister urged people, particularly those involved in politics, to read Razzaq's book.

Political analyst Prof Dilara Choudhury said every political party engages in political manoeuvring, and Jamaat-e-Islami was no exception, at times aligning with the BNP and at other times with the Awami League.

“The party survives this way,” she said.

She said Jamaat needs major internal reforms to become a mainstream political party amid the country’s changing political landscape.

Speaking virtually, Prof Ali Riaz, vice chairman of the National Consensus Commission, urged people not to view the book solely through the question of Jamaat’s apology for its role in 1971, saying it should also encourage broader public discussion on Islamist politics.

“I think that if Islamist parties want to do politics, their first task should be to build a democratic state. They must accept popular sovereignty and move forward on that basis. If they can address these issues along with the mistakes of the past, then these discussions may reach a fruitful point.”

The Daily Star’s Consulting Editor Kamal Ahmed said Abdur Razzaq wrote that no party that opposed a country’s independence struggle had ever come to power there. He argued that Jamaat must resolve the 1971 issue if it wants to form a government.

Razzaq also explained why an apology had failed, noting that a section of Jamaat believed Bangladesh should maintain a special relationship with Pakistan, he added.

A draft apology was discussed in several meetings in 2016 but was rejected at the final stage after the party’s then education secretary warned that Pakistan would be displeased.

“Does that mean the party is still dependent on Pakistan? Will the party move forward by keeping Pakistan pleased? These are important questions,” Kamal further said.

Referring to data from the book, he said Jamaat’s permanent membership grew from 650 rukon (member) in 1958 to 73,045 by 2023, while the number of workers reached 639,000 during the same period.

He further said the book puts the number of Jamaat’s associate members at 23 million, while the party received around 23.4 million votes in the recent national election.

“For this reason, the simple question is, does the party not get votes from ordinary people? Does it get votes only from its workers and associate members? Or is the figure for the party’s associate members unreliable?” he asked.

Speaking virtually, former senior US diplomat John Danilowicz said the book stood out for its honesty and openness about both the past and the future.

Many of Abdur Razzaq’s well-wishers and representatives of civil society attended the event.
